notes.title: Website Flow
notes.preview: Do users care about organization...
notes.content: Do Users Care About Organization? Recently, I've been questioning whether users really care about organization in design. At first, it seems like an obvious 'yes.' However, I started wondering if what we often call 'good design' is just aesthetically pleasing, or if it actually improves user efficiency. This thought came up because one of the websites I'm maintaining was approved to become the production model, which means it's now under the scrutiny of a wider audience. This includes both technically savvy individuals and those less familiar with the details of design. While most feedback is benign, I've occasionally gotten questions like, 'Does this really need to be a separate page?' More often than not, the answer is 'no,' but it made me realize how frequently I've separated content into different pages simply because it's the traditional approach, rather than considering if it's the most efficient design for the user.

notes.title: Passwords are on borrowed time
notes.preview: Passkeys and why I finally use a password manager
notes.content:
Most people I help at work still reuse one or two passwords for everything. I get it, remembering fifty unique passwords is impossible. That is exactly why password managers exist, and why I think every person should use one.

The bigger shift coming is passkeys. Instead of a secret you type, a passkey is a key pair. The private key stays on your device and the site only stores the public key. There is nothing to phish, because there is nothing for you to type into a fake login page, and nothing useful to steal from the server.

They are not perfect yet. Syncing between ecosystems is still awkward, and account recovery is the weak point. But for anything that supports them, I am turning them on.

notes.title: It's always DNS
notes.preview: A short ode to the protocol that breaks everything
notes.content:
There is a running joke in IT: it's not DNS, there's no way it's DNS, it was DNS.

DNS turns names like cappel.li into IP addresses. When it fails, everything looks broken at once. Websites will not load, email stops, and logins time out, even though the network itself is fine. That is why it fools people. The symptoms look like an outage, not a lookup problem.

My troubleshooting order now: can I ping an IP address directly? If yes, the network is fine and I check name resolution next with nslookup or dig. Checking that one thing early has saved me a lot of time chasing the wrong problem.

notes.title: Why phishing still works
notes.preview: The weakest link is not the firewall
notes.content:
Companies spend a lot on firewalls, endpoint protection, and filtering, and phishing still gets through. The reason is simple: phishing does not attack the computer, it attacks the person.

Good phishing emails use urgency (your account will be locked), authority (a message from the IT department or the CEO), and familiarity (a shared document from a coworker). None of that trips a technical control.

The best defense I know is boring: slow down. Hover over links before clicking. Check the real sender address, not just the display name. If a message asks for credentials or money, confirm it through a separate channel. Training helps, but making it easy and normal to report suspicious emails helps more.

notes.title: MFA fatigue
notes.preview: When the second factor becomes the attack
notes.content:
Multi-factor authentication is one of the best things you can turn on. But push-based MFA has a weakness: if an attacker already has your password, they can spam login requests until you tap approve just to make the notifications stop. This is called MFA fatigue, or push bombing.

The fixes are straightforward. Use number matching, where you have to type a code shown on the login screen into your phone. Limit how many push requests can be sent in a short window. And teach people that an unexpected MFA prompt means your password is already compromised, so report it and change it.

MFA is still worth it. The point is that it is a layer, not a finish line.

notes.title: Learning Wireshark
notes.preview: Seeing what your network is actually doing
notes.content:
Wireshark is one of those tools that looks overwhelming the first time you open it. Thousands of packets scroll by and none of it makes sense.

What helped me was starting with display filters instead of trying to read everything. A few I use constantly:

dns  (just name lookups)
http  (unencrypted web traffic)
ip.addr == 192.168.1.10  (traffic to or from one host)
tcp.flags.syn == 1  (new connection attempts)

Once you filter down, patterns show up quickly: a device that phones home every few seconds, a misconfigured service retrying forever, or a lookup that fails before every slow page load. Packet captures do not lie, which makes them the best tiebreaker when two people disagree about what is wrong.

notes.title: VLANs in plain English
notes.preview: One switch, many networks
notes.content:
A VLAN lets you split one physical switch into several separate logical networks. Devices on different VLANs cannot talk to each other directly, even if they are plugged into the same hardware, unless traffic is routed between them on purpose.

Why it matters for security: you can put printers, cameras, guests, staff, and servers on separate VLANs. If a cheap IoT camera gets compromised, it does not get a free path to the file server. Every connection between segments has to go through a router or firewall, where you can control and log it.

Segmentation is not glamorous, but it turns one big flat network where one mistake exposes everything into smaller rooms with locked doors.

notes.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Month
notes.preview: Four habits that cover most of the risk
notes.content:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, so here is the short version of what I tell friends and family. Most real-world compromises come down to a few basics:

1. Use a password manager and unique passwords.
2. Turn on MFA everywhere it is offered, especially email.
3. Install updates. Most attacks use vulnerabilities that already have patches.
4. Be suspicious of urgency. Real organizations rarely need something from you in the next ten minutes.

None of this is advanced. That is the point. Attackers usually go after the easy targets, and these four habits make you a lot less easy.

notes.title: Least privilege
notes.preview: Nobody needs admin all the time
notes.content:
The principle of least privilege means every user, service, and program gets only the access it needs to do its job, and nothing more.

It sounds obvious, but in practice people end up with admin rights because it is convenient. One installer needed it once, so the account kept it forever. That convenience is exactly what malware is looking for. Code running as a standard user can do some damage. Code running as an administrator can do almost anything.

In Active Directory this means separate admin accounts, group-based permissions instead of one-off grants, and actually removing access when someone changes roles. It is not exciting work, but it limits the damage from almost every other kind of mistake.

notes.title: The xz backdoor
notes.preview: A supply chain attack that almost worked
notes.content:
Looking back on big security stories, the xz utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) is still the one I think about most. A contributor spent a long time earning trust in a small but widely used open source compression project, then slipped a backdoor into release tarballs that could affect SSH on some Linux distributions.

It was caught almost by accident. A Microsoft engineer, Andres Freund, noticed SSH logins taking slightly longer than they should and kept digging.

The lesson for me is that supply chain security is a people problem as much as a code problem. Critical projects are often maintained by one or two volunteers who are burned out. Attackers know that. Supporting maintainers and checking what actually ships in release artifacts matters as much as scanning code.

notes.title: Home lab goals for 2026
notes.preview: What I want to build this year
notes.content:
New year, new list of things to break on purpose. A home lab is the best way I know to learn security, because you can make mistakes without anyone getting hurt.

On my list for this year:
- A proper segmented network with separate VLANs for lab, personal, and IoT devices.
- A small SIEM to collect logs from everything and practice writing detections.
- A deliberately vulnerable Active Directory setup to practice attacks and then the matching defenses.
- Better documentation, so I can rebuild everything from notes instead of memory.

The goal is not perfect infrastructure. It is understanding why each piece exists and what happens when it is missing.

notes.title: Hashing vs encryption vs encoding
notes.preview: Three words people mix up constantly
notes.content:
These three get confused all the time, so here is how I keep them straight.

Encoding changes the format of data so it can be stored or sent, like Base64. It is not security at all. Anyone can decode it.

Encryption scrambles data with a key so only someone with the right key can read it. It is reversible on purpose. Use it when you need the original data back, like files or network traffic.

Hashing turns data into a fixed-length fingerprint and is designed to be one-way. Use it when you only need to check that something matches, like passwords. Password hashes should use slow, salted algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2, not fast ones like MD5 or plain SHA-256.

If someone says a password is "encrypted in Base64," something has gone very wrong.

notes.title: Mullvad is glitchy
notes.preview: race condition
notes.content:
Windows specific Mullvad problem: On machines where physical network adapters initialize slowly (e.g. USB ethernet, certain wifi cards, or simply slow hardware), mullvad-daemon can start before any adapter is ready. The daemon applies its WFP kill switch rules immediately on startup. When the adapter comes up moments later, it falls under those rules with no established tunnel, leaving the system in a state where all network traffic is blocked and the daemon cannot recover without a manual restart.

This is fixed through this PR on MullVads public repo

https://github.com/mullvad/mullvadvpn-app/pull/10489

notes.title: Zero trust without the buzzwords
notes.preview: Never trust, always verify
notes.content:
Zero trust gets used as a marketing term so often that it has started to sound meaningless. The core idea is simple, though.

The old model treated the internal network like a castle: once you were inside the walls, you were trusted. Zero trust drops that assumption. Every request is checked based on who you are, what device you are on, and what you are trying to reach, no matter where on the network it comes from.

In practice that means strong identity and MFA, checking device health, giving each person the smallest access they need, and segmenting the network so one compromised machine cannot reach everything. You do not buy zero trust in a box. You move toward it one control at a time.

notes.title: If it isn't logged, it didn't happen
notes.preview: Why logging is the unglamorous core of security
notes.content:
When something goes wrong, the first question is always what happened. Without logs, the honest answer is that nobody knows.

Good logging means collecting authentication events, admin actions, firewall decisions, and DNS queries in one central place, with accurate timestamps and enough retention to look back weeks later. Logs that live only on the machine that got compromised are not much help, because an attacker can delete them.

The hard part is not collecting logs but making them useful. Too many alerts and people start ignoring them. I would rather have a few high-quality detections someone actually reads than thousands of alerts nobody looks at.

notes.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule
notes.preview: Backups only count if you can restore them
notes.content:
Ransomware made backups a security topic, not just an IT chore. The classic rule still holds up:

3 copies of your data,
on 2 different types of storage,
with 1 copy offsite.

Modern ransomware goes after backups first, so I would add one more rule: at least one copy should be offline or immutable, so it cannot be changed even by an account with admin rights.

And the most important part: test your restores. A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Pick a file, a folder, or a whole system, and actually bring it back. Finding out your backups were broken during a real incident is the worst time to learn it.

notes.title: Hardening SSH in five minutes
notes.preview: Small config changes that close big doors
notes.content:
Any server with SSH open to the internet starts getting brute-force attempts within minutes. A few changes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config cut most of that risk:

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
MaxAuthTries 3
AllowUsers yourusername

Set up key-based login and confirm it works before turning off passwords, or you will lock yourself out. Generate a modern key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519.

After that, add something like fail2ban to block repeat offenders, and if possible only expose SSH through a VPN or a firewall allowlist. Restart the service with systemctl restart sshd and test from a second session before closing the first one.
